The Euler totient function counts integers 1≤a≤n with gcd(a,n)=1. The Möbius function has μ(1)=1, is zero when a prime square divides n, and equals (−1)r when n is a product of r distinct primes. Consequently
∑d∣n​μ(d)={10​n=1,n>1,​
(1)
because for n>1 the sum over squarefree divisors is (1−1)r.
The Möbius inversion formula is g(n)=∑d∣n​μ(d)f(n/d). Substituting the divisor sum defining f and collecting the coefficient of g(e) gives
∑d∣n​μ(d)f(n/d)=∑e∣n​g(e)∑d∣n/e​μ(d)=g(n).
(2)
This proof uses only finite sums, so no convergence hypothesis is needed.
Classifying 1,…,n by their greatest common divisor with n gives ∑d∣n​φ(d)=n: the class with greatest common divisor n/d contains exactly φ(d) integers. Applying the Möbius inversion formula yields
φ(n)=d∣n∑​μ(d)dn​=np∣n∏​(1−p−1).​
(3)
The Riemann zeta function is ζ(s)=∑n≥1​n−s for Res>1. Absolute convergence justifies multiplication of Dirichlet series. The divisor identity for the Möbius function gives ∑μ(n)n−s=1/ζ(s) there. For Res>2 both factors below converge absolutely, and their Dirichlet convolution is the Euler totient function:
ζ(s)ζ(s−1)​=n=1∑∞​nsφ(n)​.​
(4)

A degree-n Legendre polynomial Pn​ is orthogonal, for integration on [−1,1], to every polynomial of degree at most n−1, and has n distinct roots in (−1,1). Divide p by Pn​:
p=Pn​q+r,degq≤n−1,degr≤n−1.
(5)
The Orthogonality of Legendre polynomials gives ∫p=∫r. At every quadrature node xj​, p(xj​)=r(xj​). The assumed exactness for r therefore proves exactness up to degree 2n−1, the characteristic property of Gaussian quadrature.

To prove convergence of positive quadrature on continuous functions, for a continuous f, the Weierstrass approximation theorem supplies a polynomial p with ∥f−p∥∞​<ε. For every sufficiently large n, the Gaussian quadrature rule is exact for this fixed polynomial. Positivity of its weights and their sum 2 then give
​Qn​(f)−∫−11​f​≤∑j​Aj​∣f(xj​)−p(xj​)∣+∫−11​∣f−p∣≤4ε.
(8)
Since ε is arbitrary, Qn​(f)→∫−11​f. Notice that no differentiability of f is needed; uniform polynomial approximation and positivity provide the whole argument.

3G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 158 Articles: 1

Words: 158
3G OurBigBook.com
The Shannon entropy, in bits, is
H(A)=−∑a​pa​log2​pa​=log2​5−51​≈2.121928​.
(9)
For a prescribed alphabet distribution and code alphabet, an optimal code is a uniquely decodable code minimizing expected codeword length. Huffman coding produces an optimal binary prefix code, and its minimum is also the minimum among binary uniquely decodable codes.
Two optimal binary prefix codes, listing words in the order a,b,c,d,e, are
(00,01,10,110,111),(0,10,110,1110,1111).
(10)
Their length vectors are (2,2,2,3,3) and (1,2,3,4,4), and both have expected length 2.2 bits. To verify optimality rather than just equal length, run Huffman coding. First combine d,e into a node of weight 0.2. Among the resulting three weight-0.2 nodes, combining b,c and then combining the remaining weight-0.2 node with one weight-0.4 node gives the first length vector. Instead combine c with the d,e node, then combine that weight-0.4 node with b, and finally with a; this gives the second. Each step combines two smallest current weights, so both constructions are Huffman coding trees. Ties therefore allow different optimal length profiles.

Writing yi​ for the observed counts, independence of the Poisson distributions gives the log-likelihood
ℓ(β)=∑i=1n​{yi​βxi​−eβxi​−log(yi​!)}.
(11)
Its score function and negative second derivative are
U(β)=∑i​xi​(yi​−eβxi​),J(β)=∑i​xi2​eβxi​.
(12)
Unless all xi​ vanish, J(β)>0, so the log-likelihood is strictly concave. Use Newton method, starting from a finite β0​, with
βr+1​=βr​+∑i​xi2​eβr​xi​∑i​xi​(yi​−eβr​xi​)​.​
(13)
Stop when the score function or the change in β is small; a reduced step can ensure that the log-likelihood increases. Any finite zero of the score function is the unique maximum-likelihood estimator.
Existence needs a qualification. If the nonzero xi​ include both signs, U decreases from +∞ to −∞, so a finite root exists. If all nonzero xi​ are positive, a finite root exists exactly when ∑i​xi​yi​>0; otherwise the supremum is approached as β→−∞. The corresponding condition for all negative xi​ is ∑i​xi​yi​<0, with a supremum at +∞ otherwise. When all xi​=0, the parameter is unidentifiable. These cases explain when the iterative algorithm actually has a finite estimate to find.

5E OurBigBook.com
At a positive spatially homogeneous equilibrium point, v=u2 and 2+u−v=0. Hence (u,v)=(2,4). The reaction Jacobian matrix there is
J=(24a​−2−a​),trJ=2−a,detJ=6a.
(14)
The two-dimensional Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion gives strict linear asymptotic stability for a>2, and instability for 0<a<2.
For a spatial mode with s=k2, the reaction-diffusion linearization is Js​=J−diag(s,ds). When a>2, its trace is negative for every s≥0, while
D(s)=detJs​=ds2+(a−2d)s+6a.
(15)
A growing mode exists precisely when this quadratic is negative at some s>0. Its minimum must occur at positive s, and must be strictly negative, giving
2d>a,(2d−a)2>24ad.
(16)
With z=d/a, the latter inequality becomes 4z2−28z+1>0. Selecting the root compatible with 2d>a yields the Turing instability threshold
d>(27​+23​)a.​
(17)
The unstable band is
2d2d−a−(2d−a)2−24ad​​<k2<2d2d−a+(2d−a)2−24ad​​.
(18)
On a bounded domain a boundary condition must permit a mode in this band. Equality at the threshold gives a neutral mode, not positive growth.
At a=2, the homogeneous linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues, so it is not strictly linearly asymptotically stable. If “stable” is read as nonlinear stability, the boundary deserves attention. Put x=u−2, y=(v−4−x)/3​, and x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ. The exact equations give r˙=r2F(θ), θ˙=ω+rG(θ), where ω=23​,
F=−3​cos2θsinθ​+cosθsin2θ,G=3​2cos3θ​+cos2θsinθ+3​cosθsin2θ.
(19)
Expanding dr/dθ through cubic order, ∫02π​F=0 cancels the quadratic displacement. The correction from the quadratic change in r also integrates to zero, because it is proportional to (∫F)2. Since ∫02π​FG=π/(23​), the Poincaré return map is
r⟼r−243​π​r3+O(r4).
(20)
This cubic return-map stability of a weak focus shows that a=2 is a weak attracting focus. The strict linear range used in the Turing instability calculation is a>2; the positive homogeneous equilibrium is also nonlinearly asymptotically stable at the boundary a=2. For that boundary, trJs​=−(1+d)s<0 for every nonzero spatial mode. The same strict Turing instability threshold and unstable band therefore also apply there, with the homogeneous mode understood through nonlinear stability.

Solution

Words: 147
6B OurBigBook.com
Analytic continuation extends a holomorphic function by holomorphic elements agreeing on overlaps; along a path, a chain of overlapping neighbourhoods transports the initial element. The identity theorem makes compatible continuation unique on connected overlaps, although different paths can lead to different branches.
Choose the principal complex logarithm and the slit domain D=C∖[1,∞). On D, the function
h(z)=−zLog(1−z)​
(21)
is holomorphic, with the removable value h(0)=1. The domain D is simply connected, so h has a primitive and its integral from 0 to z is independent of the path in D. For ∣z∣<1, the uniformly convergent power series on compact subdiscs gives
f(z)=∫0z​h(u)du=∫0z​∑n≥1​nun−1​du=∑n≥1​n2zn​.
(22)
Therefore f is a single-valued analytic continuation of the dilogarithm to C∖[1,∞). The apparent problem at 0 is removable; 1 is a genuine branch point, even though the function has a finite one-sided limit there, because its derivative has a logarithmic singularity. Other cuts from 1 to infinity give corresponding branches.

L3​=pψ​=I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ),Lz​=pϕ​=I1​ϕ˙​sin2θ+L3​cosθ.
(23)

E=2I1​​θ˙2+2I1​​ϕ˙​2sin2θ+2I3​L32​​+Mglcosθ.

For nonvertical uniform precession of a heavy symmetric top, write ϕ˙​=Ω and fix θ. The θ Euler-Lagrange equation reduces to
I1​cosθΩ2−I3​ω3​Ω+Mgl=0.​
(27)
For cosθ=0 its solutions are
Ω=2I1​cosθI3​ω3​±I32​ω32​−4I1​Mglcosθ​​.
(28)
For 0<θ<π/2, uniform precession therefore requires ∣ω3​∣≥2I1​Mglcosθ​/I3​. For π/2<θ<π, the discriminant is positive for every spin, including zero. At θ=π/2, the condition is Ω=Mgl/(I3​ω3​), requiring nonzero spin. Once this condition holds, choose Lz​=I1​Ωsin2θ+L3​cosθ and ψ˙​=ω3​−Ωcosθ; both cyclic equations are then satisfied. The exactly vertical configurations are also solutions for arbitrary spin, but the azimuthal member of the Euler angles is degenerate there, so their existence is separate from this nonvertical discriminant condition.

cs2​=dρdP​=34C​ρ1/3=cˉs2​t−2/3,cˉs2​=34C​(6πG)−1/3.

δ¨+3t4​δ˙+t2cˉs2​k2−2/3​δ=0.

9I (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 328 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 328
9I OurBigBook.com
Sperner's lemma says that a triangulated triangle whose vertices are labelled 1,2,3, with each outer vertex having its own label and each boundary edge using only its endpoint labels, contains a small triangle with all three labels. In fact the number of such triangles is odd. Count incidences of small triangles with edges labelled 1,2. Interior edges contribute twice. On the outer 1,2 edge, the number of changes between these labels is odd; the other two outer edges contribute zero. A small triangle contributes one incidence if it has all three labels, two if it uses both 1,2 but not 3, and zero otherwise. The total parity proves the assertion.
The resulting no-retraction theorem is: there is no continuous retraction of a closed disc onto its boundary. Work first with a closed triangle P. If r:P→∂P fixes the boundary, colour each vertex of increasingly fine triangulations by an index of a largest barycentric coordinate of r(v). The largest coordinate is at least 1/3; on the boundary the colouring satisfies Sperner's lemma. Choose a tricoloured small triangle in each triangulation. By compactness and shrinking mesh, a subsequence of their three vertices converges to one point x. Continuity forces all three barycentric coordinates of r(x) to be at least 1/3, so r(x) is the triangle's centre, contradicting r(x)∈∂P. A homeomorphism of a disc with P proves the disc assertion.
Brouwer fixed-point theorem states that every continuous self-map F of a closed disc has a fixed point. If it had none, the ray from F(x) through x would meet the boundary beyond x, continuously in x. That intersection defines a retraction, since a boundary point is already the outgoing intersection. This contradicts the no-retraction theorem.
Finally fix y∈R2 and define Fy​(x)=y+x−g(x). The displacement bound implies ∥Fy​(x)−y∥≤K, so Fy​ maps the closed radius-K disc centred at y into itself. Brouwer fixed-point theorem gives Fy​(x)=x, which is exactly g(x)=y. Since y was arbitrary, g is surjective.

Solution

Words: 374
10G OurBigBook.com
In RSA, choose N=pq with distinct large primes, an exponent e coprime to φ(N), and d satisfying ed≡1(modφ(N)). Publish (N,e) and keep d secret. Encrypt a residue m as c=memodN and decrypt by cdmodN. Fermat's little theorem on each prime and the Chinese remainder theorem prove decryption, including messages not coprime to N.
A customer knows a nonzero multiple M=ed−1 of φ(N). Write M=2st with t odd. Choose a base a at random. A nontrivial gcd(a,N) already factors N. Otherwise compute at,a2t,…,a2st modulo N. The last entry is 1. If the first occurrence of 1 is preceded by z≡±1(modN), then
gcd(z−1,N) is a nontrivial factor of N.​
(33)
Indeed, the two prime components of this square root of 1 must have opposite signs. This procedure succeeds for some bases: by the Chinese remainder theorem, choose a base whose component modulo p has order 2 and whose component modulo q has order 1. Its odd t-th power is already a nontrivial square root of 1. Trying bases therefore gives an explicit factoring algorithm, and repeated random choices give the usual efficient attack. More precisely, if the two components' orders have different powers of 2, the procedure succeeds. For a uniform element of a cyclic group with 2-part 2r, those order valuations have probabilities 2−r for 0 and 2j−1−r for 1≤j≤r. Independence of the two prime components shows that equal valuations have probability at most 1/2. Thus a random unit succeeds with probability at least 1/2. Once N is factored, every customer's private exponent is computable. The exceptional ed=1 is an identity cipher and is already insecure.
For the outsider's RSA common-modulus attack, find integers a,b with ae1​+be2​=1 by Bézout's identity. For a unit message,
m≡c1a​c2b​(modN),​
(34)
using modular inverses for negative powers. If a ciphertext is a nonzero nonunit, its greatest common divisor with N factors N instead; zero ciphertext corresponds to the zero message for a squarefree modulus. The common message is recoverable without a private key. For a generic unit message this alone does not supply the factorization or all private keys, so it does not demonstrate a complete break for unrelated messages. The nonunit case does give that stronger break.

For Res>1, expand (et−1)−1=∑n≥1​e−nt. Absolute convergence of the integrated series follows from the same expression with Res in place of s. Integrating termwise and substituting u=nt gives
∫0∞​et−1ts−1​dt=∑n≥1​n−sΓ(s)=Γ(s)ζ(s).
(35)
This proves the Mellin transform representation of the Riemann zeta function.
Take the Hankel contour along the lower side of the negative axis towards zero, around zero counterclockwise, and back along the upper side. For Res>1 the small-circle contribution tends to zero. On the lower and upper rays, respectively, argt=−π,+π, so the two integrals combine to
∫H​e−t−1ts−1​dt=(e−iπ(s−1)−eiπ(s−1))∫0∞​ex−1xs−1​dx=2isin(πs)Γ(s)ζ(s).
(36)
The gamma reflection formula now proves agreement of the two representations. At an integer s=m≥2, the contour integral has a zero while Γ(1−s) has a pole: their product is interpreted by its finite limit, equal to ζ(m), not by multiplying literal zero and infinity.
For nonpositive integers the integrand is single-valued, and the contour closes around zero. Since
e−t−11​=−t1​−21​+O(t),
(37)
the residue of t−1/(e−t−1) is −1/2, giving ζ(0)=−1/2. Also
e−t−11​+21​=−21​coth(t/2)
(38)
is odd. Its Laurent series therefore has only odd powers. Multiplication by t−2n−1 cannot produce a t−1 term, and the subtracted constant cannot do so when n≥1. Hence the contour integral vanishes and ζ(−2n)=0 for every positive integer n.

dH=q˙​dp−Lq​dq−Lt​dt,
(39)
because the dq˙​ terms cancel. With the Euler-Lagrange equation p˙​=Lq​, this gives Hamilton's equations
q˙​=Hp​,p˙​=−Hq​.​

In particular Hq​=−Lq​ at corresponding velocities, so a cyclic coordinate for the Lagrangian is also cyclic for the Hamiltonian.

H=2mpx2​+(py​−qBx)2+pz2​​+qEy.​

The graph Ramsey number R(s,t) is the least N for which every graph on N vertices has a clique of size s or an independent set of size t; R(s)=R(s,s) is the diagonal Ramsey number. The base cases are R(2,t)=t and R(s,2)=s.
Assume the smaller parameters already have finite graph Ramsey numbers, and take N=R(s−1,t)+R(s,t−1). For any vertex, either its neighbourhood has at least R(s−1,t) vertices, or its nonneighbourhood has at least R(s,t−1) vertices. In the first case it contains an independent t-set, or an (s−1)-clique which extends with the chosen vertex. In the second it contains an s-clique, or a (t−1)-independent set which extends with that vertex. Induction proves existence and
R(s,t)≤R(s−1,t)+R(s,t−1).​

One has [L:LH]=∣H∣ and [LH:K]=[Gal(L/K):H]. The field LH is Galois over K exactly when H is normal; then its Galois group is the quotient by H.

A covering map is a continuous surjection p:X→X for which each point has an open neighbourhood U with p−1(U) a disjoint union of open sets, each mapped homeomorphically onto U. A connected simply connected covering space is a universal cover.
There is a necessary connectedness qualification in the printed conclusion. Let A0​ be the path component of a0​ in A. Then p(A)=A0​: one inclusion follows by projecting paths, and the other by lifting a path in A0​ from a0​. Thus the asserted surjection onto all of A requires A to be path connected. Without it, take p to be the identity of R and A to be two disjoint intervals; a selected component cannot cover both.
To prove the assertion about a component of a pulled-back universal cover, choose an evenly covered neighbourhood U in X. Local path connectedness of A supplies a path-connected relatively open neighbourhood V⊆U∩A0​. Each inverse sheet over V is path connected, so it lies wholly in A or is disjoint from it. These sheets evenly cover V under p∣A​. Therefore p∣A​:A→A0​ is a covering map.
Under the classification of connected covering spaces, its subgroup consists of based loops in A0​ whose lifts close at a0​. A loop viewed in X closes in the universal cover exactly when its class in π1​(X,a0​) is trivial. Hence the subgroup is
p∗​π1​(A,a0​)=ker{π1​(A,a0​)i∗​​π1​(X,a0​)}.​
(60)
Here π1​(A,a0​)=π1​(A0​,a0​), so the subgroup formula itself needs no change. Injectivity of the covering's induced fundamental-group map is the usual homotopy-lifting property.

A linear map T:X→Y between normed spaces is a bounded linear operator if ∥Tx∥≤C∥x∥ for one finite C and every x. This implies ∥Tx−Ty∥≤C∥x−y∥, hence continuity. Conversely, continuity at zero supplies δ>0 such that ∥x∥<δ implies ∥Tx∥<1. Apply this to δx/(2∥x∥) to obtain ∥Tx∥≤2∥x∥/δ for nonzero x. Thus boundedness and continuity are equivalent for linear maps.
The operator norm is ∥T∥=sup∥x∥≤1​∥Tx∥, equivalently supx=0​∥Tx∥/∥x∥. The bounded operators form a vector space, since ∥(S+T)x∥≤(∥S∥+∥T∥)∥x∥ and scalar multiples remain bounded. Taking suprema proves the triangle inequality and absolute homogeneity for the operator norm; ∥T∥=0 forces Tx=0 for every x. Thus B(X,Y) is a normed space, whether or not X,Y are complete.

20F (Riemann Surfaces)

Words: 639 Articles: 5
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 299
20F OurBigBook.com
Two holomorphic function elements represent the same germ of a holomorphic function at z if they agree on some neighbourhood of z. For a holomorphic f on an open D⊆G, set U(f,D)={[f]z​:z∈D}. These sets form a basis of a topology on the space of germs of holomorphic functions: every germ lies in one, and if a germ lies in two, equality of the representatives on a smaller neighbourhood supplies a basis of a topology set in their intersection. Declaring arbitrary unions of basis of a topology sets open therefore gives a topology.
Different base points are separated by disjoint small discs in G. If two different germs have the same base point, choose representatives on one connected small disc. Their sheets are disjoint: any common germ elsewhere on that disc would force equality throughout the disc by the identity theorem. This proves the Hausdorff property.
The projection π([f]z​)=z maps each sheet U(f,D) homeomorphically onto D. Use these maps as complex charts. On overlaps their transition functions are the identity, hence holomorphic; thus each connected component is a Riemann surface, and π is a local biholomorphism, an analytic germ projection. For completeness, second countability of a component follows by following continuation chains through a countable basis of a topology of rational discs: starting at one germ, finite chains of such discs give only countably many continuation sheets, by uniqueness on overlaps, and they cover every germ in that component.
A complete analytic function consists of all germs reachable from one initial germ by analytic continuation. The supplied path-lifting equivalence identifies these with its path component. Since the germ space is locally path connected, connected components and path components agree. Thus its continuation surface is exactly one component GF​.
A local biholomorphism need not evenly cover the whole base; the germ projection is an analytic covering in this local sense. The examples below distinguish a genuine regular covering map from a surjective nonregular projection, with the meaning of regular stated explicitly.

Take G=C∗ and the complete analytic function generated by a logarithm germ. Its continuation surface identifies with C via w↦[log]z​ with z=ew and logarithm value w. Thus π(w)=ew. It is a universal cover; the deck transformations w↦w+2πin act transitively on each fibre, so it is also a regular covering map in the deck-transitive sense. It is not bijective, since every nonzero z has infinitely many logarithm values. It also meets the alternative convention in which “regular” merely requires an evenly covered neighbourhood at each base point.

A surjective inverse-polynomial germ projection without even covering comes from the inverse of P(w)=w3−3w over G=C. Consider R=C∖{−1,1}, with π(w)=P(w). Since P′(w)=3(w2−1)=0 on R, each w defines a holomorphic inverse germ of P at P(w). This identifies R with a component of the space of germs of holomorphic functions: inverse germs continue along paths in R, and the holomorphic identity P(f(z))=z persists under continuation. A germ with value ±1 cannot exist, because differentiating that identity would give P′(±1)f′(z)=1. Since R is connected, all its inverse germs belong to one complete analytic function.
The projection is surjective. A generic value has three distinct regular preimages; the critical values 2,−2 each retain a simple regular preimage, respectively 2,−2, even after their double critical preimages −1,1 are removed. Thus fibre size drops from 3 to 1 at these values, making an evenly covered neighbourhood impossible. This is surjective but not a regular topological covering.
If “regular” is specifically used for deck transitivity among genuine coverings, there is also a genuine nonnormal example. Remove the critical values from the base and all their preimages from the source:
G=C∖{−2,2},R=C∖{−2,−1,1,2},π(w)=w3−3w.

This is a connected three-sheeted analytic covering. A small loop about each critical value swaps the two roots meeting there. The two swaps are distinct and generate S3​ (connectedness also forces transitive monodromy). The stabilizer of one sheet is an order-2 subgroup, which is not normal in S3​. The classification of connected covering spaces therefore shows this covering is not regular in the deck-transitive sense. Either convention has a fully explicit example.

1=∑j​aj​(x,t)ij​(x)+b(x,t)(1−tf(x)),ij​∈I.

An immersion ϕ:U→R3 has differential of rank 2, equivalently linearly independent ϕu​,ϕv​. It has isothermal coordinates when its first fundamental form has E=G>0, F=0. A minimal surface has zero mean curvature.
For an isothermal immersion, differentiation of E=G and F=0 gives
(ϕuu​+ϕvv​)⋅ϕu​=21​Eu​+Fv​−21​Gu​=0,
(66)
and similarly its scalar product with ϕv​ is zero. Its normal component is e+g. The given mean curvature formula reduces to H=(e+g)/(2E), so
ϕuu​+ϕvv​=2EHn.​
(67)
Thus an isothermal immersion is minimal exactly when each coordinate is a harmonic function.
An explicit example is the Enneper surface, parametrized on R2 by
ϕ(u,v)=(u−u3/3+uv2, v−v3/3+u2v, u2−v2).
(68)
Every coordinate has zero Laplacian. Direct differentiation gives ϕu​⋅ϕv​=0 and ∣ϕu​∣2=∣ϕv​∣2=(1+u2+v2)2>0. Thus it is an isothermal immersion and is minimal everywhere.
It is not an open subset of any of the three listed surfaces. The parameter points (3​,0) and (−3​,0) both map to (0,0,3), but their tangent planes differ: ϕu​=(−2,0,±23​) while ϕv​=(0,4,0). A plane, catenoid, or helicoid is an embedded smooth surface with a unique tangent plane at each point. If our whole image lay in any one of them, both rank-2 tangent planes at this point would have to equal its tangent plane, a contradiction.

A rate-λ Poisson process is a counting process starting at zero, with right-continuous nondecreasing integer-valued paths, independent stationary increments, and Nt​−Ns​∼Pois(λ(t−s)) for 0≤s<t. Its jumps have size one almost surely.
For independent Poisson processes N,M, increments of N+M on disjoint intervals are independent, because all the corresponding increments of the two processes are jointly independent. On an interval of length t, multiplying their probability generating functions gives
exp(λt(z−1))exp(μt(z−1))=exp((λ+μ)t(z−1)).
(74)
Thus the increment is Poisson with mean (λ+μ)t. The path requirements hold, and independent processes almost surely have no simultaneous jumps. Therefore N+M is a Poisson process of rate λ+μ.

Bob at rest far away has dτB​/dt≃1. Thus the ratio of ageing rates is
k2=1−3rs​/(2r)1​=2r−3rs​2r​.​
(120)
For Alice's stable orbit r>3rs​, the denominator factor exceeds 1/2, proving k<2​. Both gravitational time dilation and Alice's orbital motion enter this proper-time ratio.

Solution

Words: 119
i OurBigBook.com
Near the closest point, in X=x−Ut, the gap is h(X)≃h0​+X2/(2a). The horizontal length scale is ℓ=2ah0​​, up to an inessential constant. Thus the aspect ratio h0​/ℓ≪1 follows from h0​≪a. The lubrication approximation assumes an incompressible Newtonian fluid, no slip on the surfaces, slow variation of the gap, and negligible inertia relative to transverse viscous stress:
μℓρUh02​​≪1.​
(121)
This is the reduced Reynolds-number condition; it is weaker than requiring a Reynolds number based on ℓ to be small. In the cylinder frame the geometry and flow are steady. Pressure is uniform across the narrow gap to leading order, and equal ambient pressures far to either side close the model. The calculation assumes a full liquid film; cavitation would change that pressure condition.

ii

Words: 84 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 84
ii OurBigBook.com
Reflection about the closest point leaves the gap geometry unchanged and reverses the direction of translation. The linear Stokes equations make the excess pressure change sign when the imposed velocity changes sign. Combining reflection with this linearity shows that pressure is odd in X. Its leading normal force on the stationary plane therefore cancels between the two sides, giving ey​⋅F=0 in the lubrication limit. Normal viscous stresses are of smaller order in the aspect ratio. This uses symmetry only, rather than a pressure calculation.

iii

iii OurBigBook.com
In the laboratory frame the lower wall has velocity zero and the cylinder surface has velocity U. Solving μuyy​=pX​ with these no-slip conditions gives
u(X,y)=hUy​+2μpX​​y(y−h).​
(122)
The relative velocity in the cylinder frame is u−U. Its flux is constant by incompressibility:
q=−2Uh​−12μh3pX​​.
(123)
Equal pressures at the two infinities require ∫pX​dX=0. Put Ij​=∫h−jdX; then q=−(U/2)I2​/I3​. With X=ℓs and h=h0​(1+s2), the given integrals yield I2​/I3​=4h0​/3. Hence q=−2Uh0​/3 and
pX​=h32μU(4h0​−3h)​.​
(124)
Indeed p=2μUX/h2 has this derivative and tends to ambient pressure at both ends. The distinction between the constant comoving flux and the varying laboratory flux is necessary because the gap translates.

iv OurBigBook.com
The fluid's tangential traction on the lower stationary surface is τ=μuy​∣y=0​ in the positive x direction. Using the pressure gradient found above gives
τ=hμU​−2h​pX​=4μU(h1​−h2h0​​).
(125)
The drag on a plane beneath a translating cylinder follows by integrating along the wall:
ex​⋅F=4μUh0​ℓ​(π−2π​)=2πμUh0​2a​​​
(126)
per unit cylinder-axis length. This is the force on the lower surface, so its direction follows the cylinder's translation.

36B (Waves)

Words: 286 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 286
36B OurBigBook.com
The linear elastic wave equation is ρutt​=(λ+μ)∇(∇⋅u)+μΔu. For a shear-horizontal wave, take u=(0,v(x,z,t),0) with no y dependence. Its divergence vanishes, and
vtt​=cs2​(vxx​+vzz​),cs​=μ/ρ​.
(127)
Rigid fixed boundaries require v=0 at z=0,h. The modes are v=Asin(qn​z)cos(kx−ωn​t) with qn​=nπ/h, n=1,2,…, and
ωn​(k)=cs​k2+qn2​​,ωn,cut​=cs​qn​.​
(128)
There is no n=0 displacement mode with these clamped boundary conditions. For k>0, the phase velocity and group velocity are
c(k)=cs​kk2+qn2​​​,cg​(k)=cs​k2+qn2​​k​.​
(129)
The phase velocity decreases from infinity to cs​, while the group velocity increases from zero to cs​; their product is cs2​.
For a mode of frequency ω, the appropriate time and cross-sectional average is ⟨A⟩=ω/(2πh)∫02π/ω​∫0h​Adzdt, per unit transverse width. Its average kinetic energy density is ρA2ω2/8. The only nonzero strains are exy​=eyx​=vx​/2 and eyz​=ezy​=vz​/2, while ekk​=0. Thus the elastic energy density is μ(vx2​+vz2​)/2, whose average is μA2(k2+qn2​)/8. The dispersion relation proves equality of average kinetic and elastic energies.
For the ray asymptotics of a clamped elastic waveguide mode, expand the localized initial displacement in transverse sine modes and Fourier transform in x. For a displacement released from rest, each mode evolves with cos(ωn​(k)t). At x=Vt the oscillatory phases are t(kV±ωn​(k)). If 0<∣V∣<cs​, one phase has a stationary point with
∣k∗​∣=cs2​−V2​qn​∣V∣​,ωn′′​(k∗​)>0.
(130)
The stationary phase method gives a generic oscillatory amplitude proportional to t−1/2 for each contributing mode. If the initial Fourier coefficient vanishes at the stationary point, that mode can decay faster; smooth localized data make the modal sum well behaved. If ∣V∣>cs​, there is no stationary point. Repeated integration by parts gives rapid decay for smooth rapidly decaying data; for initially compactly supported displacement, finite propagation speed makes the displacement on that ray exactly zero after a sufficiently long time. These are the requested subsonic and super-shear-speed regimes.

37E (Numerical Analysis)

a

Words: 142 Articles: 1
37E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 142
a OurBigBook.com
Order the interior grid values into a vector. The coefficient matrix has diagonal 4+ch2 and off-diagonal entries −1 at horizontal and vertical neighbours, with boundary values already zero. Every row is strictly diagonally dominant because c>0. The standard convergence theorem for strict diagonal dominance gives convergence of both the Jacobi method and the Gauss-Seidel method. The matrix is also symmetric positive definite.
For D=(4+ch2)I, the weighted Jacobi method is u(r+1)=u(r)+ωD−1(b−Au(r)), with iteration matrix Hω​=I−ωD−1A. The sine-product grid eigenvectors give
λk,l​=1−ω4+ch24{sin2(πkh/2)+sin2(πlh/2)}+ch2​,1≤k,l≤m.​
(131)
These weighted Jacobi eigenvalues for a square Dirichlet grid determine convergence. All eigenvalues of A are positive. Thus for fixed h convergence requires 0<ω<2(4+ch2)/amax​, where amax​=8cos2(πh/2)+ch2. As h↓0, this upper bound tends to 1 from above. Any fixed ω>1 therefore fails on sufficiently fine grids; ω≤0 also fails. Consequently 0<ω≤1 is necessary for all mesh sizes, and it is sufficient, since amax​<2(4+ch2) for every finite grid.

b

Words: 205 Articles: 1
37E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 205
b OurBigBook.com
A multigrid method combines a fine-grid smoother with a coarse-grid correction. Starting with uh​, apply a few smoothing iterations, compute rh​=bh​−Ah​uh​, restrict this residual to a coarser grid, and approximately solve AH​eH​=Rrh​. Prolong the coarse error and update uh​←uh​+PeH​, then post-smooth. The coarse solve is itself performed recursively, with a direct solve at the coarsest level; visiting each coarser level once gives a V-cycle. The smoother damps rapidly varying error, while error smooth on the fine grid is efficiently represented and corrected on the coarse grid.
For ordinary Jacobi, ω=1, the highest-frequency sine-product error has eigenvalue approaching −1, not zero. In particular for the discrete Poisson equation it is −cos(πh), whose magnitude approaches one. This nearly alternating error changes sign between sweeps but is barely damped, and ordinary coarse-grid restriction does not represent it well. Thus with the standard point-Jacobi smoother and coarse-grid transfers one chooses ω=1, usually 0<ω<1, for fast multigrid convergence. For example ω=2/3 makes the extreme high-frequency eigenvalue approach −1/3. Convergence of Jacobi as a standalone iteration is therefore insufficient to guarantee that it is an effective smoother. This conclusion concerns that standard multigrid choice; other smoothers or specially designed transfers can change it.
